The graph shows a portion of the curve y=cos⁡x and y=−12. Which of the following generates the x-values of all of their points of intersection? Assume that n is an integer.

a
x=5π6+2nπ,x=7π6+2nπ
b
x=2π3+2nπ,x=4π3+2nπ
c
x=2π3+2nπ,x=5π3+2nπ
d
x=π6+2nπ,x=11π6+2nπ
e
x=π3+2nπ,x=5π3+2nπ
Don't Know
Submit

decision.explanation: Intersections satisfy cos(x)=-1/2, which occurs at 2π/3 and 4π/3 in each period of length 2π. Thus option b gives all solutions. This tests basic trigonometric equations, a prerequisite skill absent from the supplied differential-equations topic list.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14035554/assets/8197d1111bbd4c3b8908bc12cbc58561ffd23fe06d9f9fa99f9ab815ed78733f.png)

The graph shows a portion of the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Which of the following generates the $x$-values of all of their points of intersection? Assume that $n$ is an integer.
after.worked_solution:
At the intersection points, the $y$-values are the same for both graphs. This gives the equation $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

First, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2\pi }{3}
$$

Our first solution lies in the $2$nd quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14035554/assets/ba34bf96662682ec433c3ade0bf3f118638212101a0729fe95bbae05aee8bf1e.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$  lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution for the given equation is 

$$
x=\frac{2\pi }{3}+2n\pi ,\,x=\frac{4\pi }{3}+2n\pi .
$$

Question 1
?

The graph shows a portion of the curve y=cos⁡x and y=−12. Which of the following generates the x-values of all of their points of intersection? Assume that n is an integer.

a
x=5π6+2nπ,x=7π6+2nπ
b
x=2π3+2nπ,x=4π3+2nπ
c
x=2π3+2nπ,x=5π3+2nπ
d
x=π6+2nπ,x=11π6+2nπ
e
x=π3+2nπ,x=5π3+2nπ
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the intersection points, the y-values are the same for both graphs. This gives the equation cos⁡x=−12.

First, we find the principal value: x1=arccos⁡(−12)=2π3

Our first solution lies in the 2nd quadrant and has a reference angle of θR=π3. Since cos⁡x<0, the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has θR=π3.

Since the second solution x2 lies in the 3rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

x2=π+θR=π+π3=4π3

Hence, the general solution for the given equation is x=2π3+2nπ,x=4π3+2nπ.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 6\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 6-(-7)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+y2z+C
b
f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+yz2+C
c
f(x,y,z)=sin2⁡(2x)+2y2z+C
d
f(x,y,z)=cos⁡(2x)+yz+C
e
f(x,y,z)=cos2⁡(2x)+2yz+C

decision.explanation: For f(x,y,z)=sin(2x)+y²z+C, the partial derivatives are f_x=2cos(2x), f_y=2yz, and f_z=y², matching F. Thus option a is correct. Finding a scalar potential is a multivariable-calculus prerequisite, rather than any of the supplied differential-equations topics.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,i+2yz\,j+{y}^{2}\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
after.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2yz)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) & ={y}^{2} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+C.
$$

Consider the function F(x,y,z)=2cos⁡(2x)i+2yzj+y2k. Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).

a
f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+y2z+C
b
f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+yz2+C
c
f(x,y,z)=sin2⁡(2x)+2y2z+C
d
f(x,y,z)=cos⁡(2x)+yz+C
e
f(x,y,z)=cos2⁡(2x)+2yz+C
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2cos⁡(2x),∂f∂y=2yz,∂f∂z=y2

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫2cos⁡(2x)dx=sin⁡(2x)+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=2yz into account, we obtain ∂g∂y=2yz

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫(2yz)dy=y2z+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=y2z+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+y2z+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=y2+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=y2 into account, we obtain y2+h′(z)=y2h′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(2x)+y2z+C.

after.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{2t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3t{e}^{t} \\ -t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})\cdot (-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{-t} & 3{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ \frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}27(t-1)+(3t+1) \\ 27(t-1)+3(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}30t-26 \\ 36t-24\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: At a geological site, an object is found with $75%$ of its original chlorine-36 content. Given that the half-life of chlorine-36 is $301$ thousand years, approximately how old is the object?
after.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=301$ thousand years, we have

$$
301=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{301}.
$$

So, we have

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=0.75{M}_{0}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
0.75{M}_{0}={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.75{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ 0.75\cancel{{M}_{0}} & =\cancel{{M}_{0}}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ 0.75 & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75) & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{301} \\ t & =-\frac{301\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.75)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈125.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the object is approximately $125$ thousand years old.

after.worked_solution:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-{x}^{3}}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-{x}^{3}}^{a}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{a}^{-{x}^{3}}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $a$ is any constant number between $-{x}^{3}$ and $x.$

The integrand ${t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying the FTC II gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{a}^{-{x}^{3}}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{-{x}^{3}}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{a}^{x}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({\int }_{a}^{u}{t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t)+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-(-3{x}^{2}){u}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{x}^{2}{(-{x}^{3})}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-{x}^{3})+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{x}^{14}\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{3}+{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the substitution $u=-{x}^{3}.$

Finally, we can compute ${f}^{′}(1).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & =3(1)^{14}\operatorname{cos}⁡{1}^{3}+{1}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡1 \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡1+\operatorname{cos}⁡1 \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡1.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the flowchart below to determine which tests to use for each series.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14035554/assets/3aa7f0243efeab51d00aa9694dd018245f7ca4664cc1a5fdf4e646aebb61536e.png)

With that in mind, let's test each series in turn.

- For the first series, we use the alternating series test. Observe that 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}
$$

is positive and decreasing for all $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, by the alternating series test, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!}
$$

is also convergent.

- For the second series, we use the limit comparison test. Let 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}\,{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Working out the necessary limit, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n}}{{b}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}÷\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}\cdot \sqrt{n}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2n}{n+2}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2}{(1+\frac{2}{n})}) \\  & =\frac{2}{1+0} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $L=2$ is positive and finite. Now, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

is divergent by the $p$-series test. So, the series 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}
$$

is also divergent by the limit comparison test.

- For the final series, we use the $n$th term test for divergence. Let 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}
$$

Then, we have ${lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\infty ,$ since the polynomial in the numerator grows faster than the polynomial in the denominator. Therefore, by the $n$th term test, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}
$$

is divergent.

In conclusion, only series I converges.

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes become vertical as $y\to -2$ only. 

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}} \\ {y}^{′} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{y+2} \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{3}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the slopes become horizontal as $y\to \infty .$

Of the remaining options, the only two that give this behavior are

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}} \\ {y}^{′} & =-\frac{3}{y+2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, the slopes of the slope field are positive for all $y\ne -2.$ 

Therefore, the equation ${y}^{′}=-\frac{3}{y+2}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation are negative for $y>-2.$

On the other hand, the equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that the right-hand side of this equation is positive for all $y\ne -2.$

So, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{(y+2)^{2}}.$

Question 9
?

Identify the differential equation that generated the slope field above.

a
y′=y2y+2
b
y′=1y2+2y
c
y′=−2y2
d
y′=1(y+2)2
e
y′=−3y+2
Don't Know
Submit
Skipped Question
EXPLANATION

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

  • First, the slopes become vertical as y→−2 only.

    Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following: y′=1(y+2)2y′=y2y+2y′=−3y+2

  • Second, the slopes become horizontal as y→∞.

    Of the remaining options, the only two that give this behavior are y′=1(y+2)2y′=−3y+2

  • Finally, the slopes of the slope field are positive for all y≠−2.

    Therefore, the equation y′=−3y+2 does not give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation are negative for y>−2.

    On the other hand, the equation y′=1(y+2)2 gives the required behavior. Notice that the right-hand side of this equation is positive for all y≠−2.

So, the correct answer is y′=1(y+2)2.

What is the coefficient of (x−1)3 in the third-degree Taylor polynomial of f(x)=e−x2 about x=1?

a
 13e
b
 3e
c
 23e
d
 16e
e
 2e
Don't Know
Submit

decision.explanation: The coefficient is f'''(1)/3!. Differentiating gives f'''(x)=(12x-8x^3)e^{-x^2}, so f'''(1)=4/e and the coefficient is 2/(3e). This tests Taylor polynomials of a given function, a prerequisite; it does not test Taylor series solutions of differential equations.

What is the coefficient of (x−1)3 in the third-degree Taylor polynomial of f(x)=e−x2 about x=1?

a
 13e
b
 3e
c
 23e
d
 16e
e
 2e
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The coefficient of (x−1)3 is 13!f(3)(1). Let's compute the necessary derivatives:

f(x)=e−x2f′(x)=−2xe−x2f″(x)=−2e−x2+4x2e−x2f‴(x)=12xe−x2−8x3e−x2 Next, we evaluate f‴(1), which gives

f‴(1)=12⋅1⋅e−12−8⋅13⋅e−12=4e−1=4e.

Therefore,

13!f‴(1)=13!⋅4e=23e.

So the coefficient of (x−1)3 is 23e.

decision.explanation: This tests solving a first-order linear ODE using an integrating factor, matching topic 877. The integrating factor is exp(∫x/6 dx)=exp(x²/12). Multiplying and integrating gives y=6+C exp(-x²/12); y(0)=5 implies C=-1, so y=6-exp(-x²/12).
